title: Using Atomic Term Symbols to Interpret Atomic Spectra
lead: Under high resolution, lines of atomic spectra that look single turn out to be groups of closely spaced lines. Spin-orbit coupling splits the levels behind them, and term symbols, with selection rules written in their quantum numbers, say which transitions make up each line of hydrogen and sodium.
objectives: Demonstrate how spin-orbit coupling is experimentally observed in atomic spectra
Use atomic terms symbols to ascribe transitions to specific angular momenta states described by atomic term symbols

exercises.prompt: Confirm that the nine term symbols in Table 8.11.1 are correct.

answer.hint: With one electron, $L = l$ and $S = \tfrac{1}{2}$; $J$ runs from $|L - S|$ to $L + S$.
answer.solution:
Hydrogen has one electron, so $S = s = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and every term is a doublet, $2S + 1 = 2$, and $L = l$. $J$ runs from $|L - S|$ to $L + S$, so $J = L \pm \tfrac{1}{2}$ when $L > 0$ and $J = \tfrac{1}{2}$ alone when $L = 0$.

  • An s electron ($l = 0$): $L = 0$, $J = \tfrac{1}{2}$, giving $^2S_{1/2}$ for 1s, 2s and 3s.
  • A p electron ($l = 1$): $L = 1$, $J = \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}$, giving $^2P_{1/2}$ and $^2P_{3/2}$ for 2p and 3p.
  • A d electron ($l = 2$): $L = 2$, $J = \tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{5}{2}$, giving $^2D_{3/2}$ and $^2D_{5/2}$ for 3d.

That is $1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9$ term symbols, as the table lists.

exercises.prompt: Confirm that the values for the degeneracy in Table 8.11.1 are correct and that the total number of states add up to 8 for n = 2 and 18 for n = 3.

parts.hint: A level with total angular momentum quantum number $J$ has $2J + 1$ values of $m_J$.

answer.solution: Each term has one state for each $m_J$ from $+J$ to $-J$, so its degeneracy is $2J + 1$: 2 for $J = \tfrac{1}{2}$, 4 for $J = \tfrac{3}{2}$ and 6 for $J = \tfrac{5}{2}$, as the table gives. For n = 2: $^2S_{1/2}$ (2) + $^2P_{1/2}$ (2) + $^2P_{3/2}$ (4) = 8. For n = 3: $^2S_{1/2}$ (2) + $^2P_{1/2}$ (2) + $^2P_{3/2}$ (4) + $^2D_{3/2}$ (4) + $^2D_{5/2}$ (6) = 18. Both equal $2n^2$, twice the $n^2$ orbitals, so coupling the spin to the orbital motion regroups the states without changing their number.

exercises.prompt: Use the Russell-Saunders selection rules to determine which transitions contribute to the $H_{\alpha}$ line in the hydrogen spectrum.

answer.hint: List the terms of n = 3 and n = 2 from Table 8.11.1. With one electron, $\Delta L$ must equal $\Delta l = \pm 1$; then check $\Delta J$.
answer.solution:
$H_\alpha$ is an electron falling from n = 3 to n = 2. Every term is a doublet, so $\Delta S = 0$ always holds. With one electron $L = l$, and $\Delta l = \pm 1$ rules out $\Delta L = 0$, so only S ↔ P and P ↔ D transitions occur. Then $\Delta J = 0, \pm 1$ leaves seven transitions:

  • $3\,^2S_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{1/2}$ and $3\,^2S_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$
  • $3\,^2P_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2S_{1/2}$ and $3\,^2P_{3/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2S_{1/2}$
  • $3\,^2D_{3/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{1/2}$, $3\,^2D_{3/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$ and $3\,^2D_{5/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$

$3\,^2D_{5/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{1/2}$ is forbidden ($\Delta J = 2$), and so are $3P \rightarrow 2P$ and $3S \rightarrow 2S$ ($\Delta l = 0$). Terms with the same $n$ and $J$ have the same energy, so the seven transitions fall at five wavenumbers, the five lines of Figure 8.11.2. The two strongest, $3\,^2D_{5/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$ and $3\,^2D_{3/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{1/2}$ (with $3\,^2P_{3/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2S_{1/2}$ at the same place), make the doublet.
